idiom_name: Iterator.unfold(init)(f) as the unfold + Iterator#foldLeft as the fold
implementation_notes: Scala 2.13's companion object provides Iterator.unfold(init)(f) - the anamorphism itself: f returns Option[(A, S)] and None terminates - and Iterator is lazy, so foldLeft consumes each element as it is produced without any intermediate collection. Because an Iterator is one-shot, the fused pipeline is its natural use: the generator and the consumer exist only for this pass. Reach for the memoized LazyList variant when the generated sequence must be traversed again, and for a plain while loop when the unfold is a trivial counter and allocation-free code matters.
code_sketch:
def countdown(n: Int): Iterator[Int] =            // coalgebra (unfold)
  Iterator.unfold(n)(s => Option.when(s > 0)((s, s - 1)))

def factorial(n: Int): Long =                     // fused fold, no collection
  countdown(n).foldLeft(1L)(_ * _)
pitfalls: Iterator is single-use: after a foldLeft the iterator is exhausted and a second fold returns the identity value silently - rebuild it with a fresh call to the unfold function.
The unfold function must return None to stop; a coalgebra that always returns Some diverges and foldLeft spins forever with no intermediate structure to inspect.
foldLeft is stack-safe for Iterator, but folding into a List (or using foldRight) reintroduces the materialized structure the hylomorphism avoids.

variants.name: LazyList.unfold + foldLeft (memoized lazy list)
variants.idiom_name: LazyList.unfold(init)(f) as the unfold + foldLeft over the memoized list
variants.implementation_notes: LazyList.unfold builds the same unfold but yields a memoized lazy list: elements are computed on demand and then retained, so the structure can be traversed more than once and shared between consumers - at the cost of holding the prefix in memory, which is exactly the heap the Iterator-based fusion avoids. Choose it when the generated sequence is part of the API or feeds several folds and re-computation would be worse than retention; choose Iterator.unfold when the point is a single fused pass. Both APIs live in the 2.13 standard library and are unchanged in Scala 3.
variants.code_sketch:
def countdown(n: Int): LazyList[Int] =           // memoised unfold
  LazyList.unfold(n)(s => Option.when(s > 0)((s, s - 1)))

def factorial(n: Int): Long =                     // fold over the lazy list
  countdown(n).foldLeft(1L)(_ * _)                  // elements are cached
pitfalls: Memoization is retention: folding a large generated LazyList keeps every element alive for the lifetime of the reference - a memory leak by design if the list is captured in a long-lived object.
A LazyList without a retained head is re-computed on each traversal, so 'memoized' only holds while a reference to the front is kept.
foldRight on a lazy list is not stack-safe for large lists; prefer foldLeft or Iterator for one-shot consumption.
